prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Do not use parentheses.

text:
On April 11, 1970, Apollo 13 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three astronauts toward what was meant to be the third landing on the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, was making his fourth spaceflight and would soon become the first person to fly to the Moon twice. Fred Haise was the lunar module pilot, a rookie in space. Jack Swigert was the command module pilot, a late replacement who joined the crew only days earlier, after the original pilot, Ken Mattingly, was exposed to German measles and grounded. The target was the Fra Mauro highlands, a rugged region scientists wanted to study.

The launch itself had a warning sign. One of the second stage engines shut down early, and the remaining engines burned longer to make up the difference. Nobody thought much of it. For two days the flight was so smooth that the public paid little attention. Networks declined to carry the crew's television broadcast on the evening of April 13, and the astronauts gave a cheerful tour of their spacecraft to a small audience. Lovell signed off with a wish for a good evening.

Fifty-five hours and about fifty-five minutes into the mission, Mission Control asked the crew to stir the oxygen and hydrogen tanks in the service module. This was routine. Swigert flipped the switch. Moments later there was a bang, and the spacecraft shuddered. Lovell had felt nothing like it. Warning lights lit up, and the electrical power began to fall. Swigert reported the now famous words, which became popularly shortened to "Houston, we've had a problem." Lovell repeated the report, and the line entered history.

The cause was hidden in the oxygen tank. Years earlier, the tank had been dropped slightly during handling, and a later change in the electrical rating of its heater was never matched by the thermostats. During ground testing, the heater ran far hotter than anyone knew and damaged the wiring insulation. When Swigert threw the switch in flight, a spark in the exposed wires ignited the Teflon insulation inside the tank. The pressure soared, and the tank burst. The blast tore away a panel of the service module and crippled the second oxygen tank. Oxygen drained into space. The fuel cells, which used oxygen to make electricity and water, began to die.

Lovell looked out a window and saw gas streaming from the side of the ship. He understood what that meant. The command module, Odyssey, would soon lose its power, and with it the crew's way home. The Moon landing was gone. The only goal now was survival.

The lunar module, Aquarius, became a lifeboat. It was designed to carry two men for two days on the Moon, and now it had to sustain three men for four. The crew moved into it and powered down Odyssey to save its remaining batteries for the final descent through the atmosphere. Mission Control, led by flight director Gene Kranz, worked through the night. Kranz and his team were determined to bring the men home, and he said that failure was not an option, a phrase later made famous by the film about the mission.

The first problem was the path. The ship was on a free return trajectory, meaning that it would swing around the Moon and head back toward Earth, but it would miss the ocean, and the trip would take too long for the supplies aboard. Controllers decided to fire the descent engine of the lunar module, an engine never meant for this task. The burn after the ship passed behind the Moon sped up the return and aimed the craft toward a Pacific splashdown. A later burn corrected small errors in the course.

Then came the problem of power and water. Aquarius had to be run on a trickle of electricity, and the crew shut down nearly everything, including the heaters and most of the computers. The cabin grew cold, falling to near freezing, and the men slept little. Water was rationed severely, and Haise developed a kidney infection from the dehydration and a fever that left him miserable. Lovell and Swigert were also tired and cold, but each carried on. Moisture condensed on the walls, and everyone worried about what would happen when the equipment warmed again.

The air was the most urgent danger. Carbon dioxide builds up in a closed cabin and becomes poisonous. The lunar module had canisters of lithium hydroxide to absorb it, but they were built for two men and began to fill. The command module had spare canisters, but they were square, and the lunar module's sockets were round. Engineers on the ground gathered the same items the crew had aboard, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, suit hoses, and duct tape, and built an adapter on the spot. They read the steps over the radio, and the astronauts made one. Carbon dioxide levels dropped, and the immediate threat eased.

Back on Earth, another team worked on the final problem, which was how to wake up Odyssey after days without power. The procedure for powering it up normally took hours of careful checks, and the batteries could not afford that. Mattingly, the astronaut who had been grounded, spent long hours in a simulator with engineers, trying and discarding sequences until they found one that worked within the limits of the batteries. Their sequence was sent to the crew.

Before reentry, the crew had to discard the damaged service module. When it drifted away, they finally saw the extent of the damage. One whole side of the module was missing, a ragged hole where a panel had been blown off. Lovell described the scene to Mission Control. Then the lunar module, Aquarius, which had saved them, was released shortly before entry. It would burn up in the atmosphere.

On April 17, the ship plunged toward Earth. Reentry always causes a blackout in radio communication for about three minutes. This time it lasted longer, as the ship came in at a slightly different angle, and the wait stretched to almost four minutes. Controllers waited in silence. The world waited with them. Then Swigert's voice returned, and parachutes appeared over the Pacific near Samoa. The crew splashed down safely and were picked up by the recovery ship, the USS Iwo Jima.

The investigation that followed blamed the incident on the oxygen tank's design and handling, and NASA changed the tanks, wiring, and procedures for later flights. The program continued, and several more missions reached the Moon. But Apollo 13 is remembered less as a failure than as a rescue. Thousands of engineers, controllers, and contractors solved one problem after another under unimaginable pressure, while three men endured the cold and the dark far from home. The mission was later called a successful failure, and the phrase fits. The landing was lost, but the lives were saved, and the story still speaks to how people can work together in a crisis.
